Well, Dr. Smith, I... I didn't actually make the appointment myself. They kind of made me come in. I work down at the freight warehouse, moving materials and stock, you know, just paying the bills since I took a break from taking my college classes. But today, things got really... well, everyone got really worked up. I guess they brought me in because of what I was doing on the floor. 

See, I was working by the loading dock, right near the main forklift lane where the big pallets come through, and I just kept... freezing. Like, my body would just stop. I'd be standing right by the forklift and I'd just freeze with my arms straight up in the air, just holding them there for a long time. And the machine, it has this backup alarm, this really specific, piercing beep, and I kept copying it. I was making the exact same beeping sounds out loud, matching the rhythm perfectly, and doing all the hand signals the ground guides use, just repeating them over and over. 

And then with the freight—when I was supposed to be stacking the boxes, I wasn't just throwing them on the pallet like they want you to. I was moving them into these strange little patterns, arranging them really specifically because they just had to go in those exact spots. The foreman and the other guys were getting so mad, they were yelling at me, literally screaming over the noise of the machinery for me to stop and just load the truck the normal way, but I just kept moving them in those patterns and making the sounds. I couldn't really stop doing it even with them yelling. So... yeah, they pulled me off the floor and brought me here.

No, no... I mean, when I was a kid? Not at all. I was just a regular kid, you know? I never did the freezing thing or cared about patterns back then. But that never happened when I was a kid. It's just recently that the patterns started actually mattering, like the boxes *have* to go in those exact spots or everything is just wrong. But I never cared about that stuff before. So no, it's definitely not from when I was little. An outside force? Like... like someone with a remote control or something? No, no, nothing like that. It's not like someone is beaming thoughts into my head or making me do it. Fevers? No, no fevers. I mean, it gets incredibly hot in the warehouse, obviously. Family history? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my family is just... normal. My dad, he manages an auto body shop out in Westlake, the one with the big faded blue sign that's been missing the 'E' for like five years now. He gets stressed out, sure, especially when the supply chain gets backed up and he's waiting on parts, like those OEM bumpers that take three weeks to ship from overseas. He'll yell and throw a wrench across the garage sometimes when he's frustrated, but that's just him blowing off steam because the customers are breathing down his neck. It's not a psychiatric condition, it's just being a mechanic, you know? 

And my mom, she's perfectly fine too. She works the morning shift at that diner over by the interstate, the one that serves breakfast all day. She's always on her feet, pouring coffee and carrying those heavy ceramic plates, so she complains about her sciatica a lot. She's actually the one who told me to get those gel inserts I bought for my work boots, because she has to wear these thick white orthopedic shoes for her shifts or her legs cramp up. But her mind? Completely sharp. She remembers the regular customers' orders before they even sit down in the booth. 

As for my grandparents... well, my dad's dad died of a massive heart attack back when I was in middle school, but that was just because he ate bacon every single morning of his life and smoked two packs of Pall Malls a day since he was sixteen. It was his heart, nothing to do with his head. And my grandma on my mom's side, she's still around, living in this little assisted living place a few towns over. She forgets where she put her reading glasses sometimes, or she'll call me by my dad's name, but she's eighty-two, so that's just what happens when you get old. It's not some big mental illness, it's just normal aging.

I already have to deal with feeling crushed and trapped in the aisles at work, I'm not going to go to a hospital and let them shove me in a tube to do it to me on my day off. So no, no blood tests, no scans, nothing abnormal on any medical charts because I haven't had any tests done. I haven't needed to. I'm just trying to manage the situation at the warehouse.

That loud, piercing beep from the forklift, the one that echoes off the corrugated metal walls and gets stuck right in the center of my forehead until I have to let it out. But not voices. I mean, I hear the guys on the floor talking, obviously. Like I hear Dave complaining about his back, or the foreman yelling over the intercom system—which, by the way, has this terrible static sound before he even starts talking, it's like this crackling noise that buzzes in your ears. But that's real, everybody hears that. And I don't see things either. I mean, I see the boxes, I see the patterns they have to be in, the exact alignment of the corners on the pallets, how the cardboard edges have to line up perfectly or the whole structure of the aisle feels wrong. But I'm not seeing ghosts or shadows or things that aren't there. It's just the warehouse, just the heavy air pressing down on my shoulders, making my arms go up, and the boxes, and the beeps. That's all. Nothing else. Just... just exactly what's there, but heavier, you know?\n\nDoctor: When you feel that 'heavy air' pressing down or feel the need to arrange the boxes in exact patterns, do you have a specific belief about why this is happening—like feeling it's controlled by an outside force, has special meaning, or is connected to something only you understand?\n\nPatient: An outside force? Like... like someone with a remote control or something? No, no, nothing like that. It's not like someone is beaming thoughts into my head or making me do it. And it doesn't mean anything special, like a secret code or a message. It's not like I'm trying to spell out words with the pallets. I don't know *why* it happens, it just... it just is. Like gravity, you know? You don't ask why gravity holds the forklift on the ground, it just does. It's just the physical reality of the space. \n\nWhen the air gets heavy—and I'm telling you, it gets so thick by those loading dock doors, especially around 2:00 PM when the sun is hitting the metal siding and the dust from the cardboard is just hanging there in the humidity—the pressure just builds up. And the boxes, they just *have* to be aligned. If the corner of one of those heavy-duty double-walled boxes, the ones we use for the automotive parts that weigh like fifty pounds each, if that corner is even a quarter-inch over the edge of the wooden pallet... the whole structure of the aisle is wrong. You can feel the tension in the air. \n\nGary, the foreman, he'll come stomping over with his clipboard—he always has this aluminum clipboard that clicks when he snaps the pen into it—and he'll yell, 'What are you doing, you're wasting time, wrap the pallet!' But he doesn't feel the weight of it. He doesn't understand that if I don't fix the corners, if I don't make the pattern exact, the pressure just keeps pressing down on my shoulders until my arms have to go up to hold it. But I don't have some crazy theory about it. It's not the government or spirits or anything. It's just the warehouse. It's just the way the boxes have to be so the air doesn't crush you. I don't know why nobody else notices it, but I'm just dealing with what's right in front of me. There's no secret meaning, it's just exactly what I'm telling you.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other physical symptoms around this time, like fevers, muscle stiffness, tremors, seizures, or unusual changes in your heart rate or blood pressure?\n\nPatient: Fevers? No, no fevers. I mean, it gets incredibly hot in the warehouse, obviously. Like, in mid-July, when all the loading bay doors are wide open but there's absolutely no cross-breeze coming off the asphalt parking lot, you just sweat right through your high-vis shirt. We have to wear these bright neon yellow ones, safety mandate, and they show sweat really bad right down the middle of your back. So I get hot, sure, but not sick-hot. Not a fever. \n\nAnd muscle stiffness... well, I'm lifting freight all day. Anyone would be a little stiff, right? When you're moving pallets of those automotive parts—like I was telling you, fifty pounds a box, sometimes sixty if it's the brake rotors—your lower back is going to feel it by the end of a ten-hour shift. But it's not like a weird, unnatural stiffness. It's just the job. I don't have tremors or the shakes or anything like that. My hands are completely steady. Honestly, they have to be steady to line up the corners of the boxes exactly right. If my hands were shaking even a little bit, I couldn't get the cardboard edges perfectly flush with the wood of the pallet, and then the whole pattern would be off, and the aisle would just feel completely wrong. So no, no shaking. And definitely no seizures. I've never passed out or had a seizure or anything scary like that. \n\nAs for my heart rate or blood pressure... I mean, it's just normal for working. Sometimes when I have to hold my arms up, you know, when the air gets too heavy and thick and I have to push back against it so it doesn't just crush down on me, my heart might beat a little faster just from the physical effort of holding my arms locked in place for so long. It takes a lot of energy to hold up that kind of pressure. But it's not like my heart is just racing out of nowhere for no reason. It's just the exertion of dealing with the weight in the aisle. I actually had to do a full physical for this job—the company makes everyone go to this occupational clinic down on 4th Street before they even let you touch the forklift—and they checked all of that. My blood pressure was totally fine. Perfect, the nurse said. So physically, I'm fine. I'm not sick. It's just the environment I'm dealing with.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any other symptoms lately, like unexplained weight changes, joint pain, skin rashes, excessive thirst, or changes in your energy or sleep that might suggest something going on with your body overall?\n\nPatient: Weight changes? No, I weigh exactly what I always weigh. I mean, I step on the scale in my bathroom sometimes—it's this old dial scale right next to a cracked tile near the sink—and it's always the same. 175, maybe 178 if I just ate. I eat the exact same thing every single day anyway, so there's no reason my weight would fluctuate. I pack a turkey sandwich, whole wheat bread, just a thin layer of mayo, because if you put too much on, the bread gets completely soggy by the time the 11:30 lunch whistle blows. And I always get a bag of those jalapeño kettle chips from the vending machine in the breakroom. The breakroom has this constant, buzzing fluorescent light that drives me crazy, but anyway, no, my weight is exactly the same as it was when I started the job. \n\nAnd joint pain... I mean, I told you about my lower back earlier, but that's just muscle fatigue. It's not my joints. My knees are perfectly fine. I made sure to buy these specific steel-toed boots, the heavy-duty Timberlands, and I even went to the pharmacy on Route 9 to get those extra gel arch support inserts. If you stand on solid concrete for ten hours without them, your heels feel like they're literally bruising from the inside out. But my joints themselves? They don't ache at all. They bend exactly how they're supposed to when I squat down to pick up the freight. Gary is always yelling over the intercom, 'lift with your legs, not your back,' so my knees do a lot of the work, but they don't hurt. \n\nSkin rashes? No, definitely not. Like I said, the high-vis shirts make you sweat a ton, and the cardboard dust is everywhere. When you rip open a new pallet of shrink wrap, this fine brown dust just poofs up and coats your forearms by the end of the shift. Sometimes that makes you itch just a tiny bit if you sweat through it, but it washes right off as soon as I get home. I use that really strong blue soap, the Irish Spring one, and it cuts right through the warehouse grime. So no, no rashes or weird spots or anything. My skin is totally normal.\n\nAs for being excessively thirsty... no, I drink a normal amount of water. It's a hot warehouse, obviously, so you have to stay hydrated. We have one of those big blue water cooler jugs over in the corner near loading bay 4, the kind you have to flip upside down into the dispenser. I'm usually the one who has to change it out because I'm the youngest guy on the floor and all the older guys act like it\n\nDoctor: Does anyone in your family—parents, siblings, or grandparents—have a history of mental illness, like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or any other psychiatric condition?\n\nPatient: Family history? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my family is just... normal. My dad, he manages an auto body shop out in Westlake, the one with the big faded blue sign that's been missing the 'E' for like five years now. He gets stressed out, sure, especially when the supply chain gets backed up and he's waiting on parts, like those OEM bumpers that take three weeks to ship from overseas. He'll yell and throw a wrench across the garage sometimes when he's frustrated, but that's just him blowing off steam because the customers are breathing down his neck. It's not a psychiatric condition, it's just being a mechanic, you know? \n\nAnd my mom, she's perfectly fine too. She works the morning shift at that diner over by the interstate, the one that serves breakfast all day. She's always on her feet, pouring coffee and carrying those heavy ceramic plates, so she complains about her sciatica a lot. She's actually the one who told me to get those gel inserts I bought for my work boots, because she has to wear these thick white orthopedic shoes for her shifts or her legs cramp up. But her mind? Completely sharp. She remembers the regular customers' orders before they even sit down in the booth. \n\nAs for my grandparents... well, my dad's dad died of a massive heart attack back when I was in middle school, but that was just because he ate bacon every single morning of his life and smoked two packs of Pall Malls a day since he was sixteen. It was his heart, nothing to do with his head. And my grandma on my mom's side, she's still around, living in this little assisted living place a few towns over. She forgets where she put her reading glasses sometimes, or she'll call me by my dad's name, but she's eighty-two, so that's just what happens when you get old. It's not some big mental illness, it's just normal aging. \n\nAnd I just have one younger sister. She's eighteen, just started her freshman year at the state college. I took a few classes there myself a couple years ago before I realized sitting in a stuffy lecture hall with those awful fluorescent lights humming overhead just wasn't for me, which is why I took the freight job instead. I just needed to be doing something physical, moving things around. But anyway, my sister is doing great, she's pledging a sorority and making the dean's list and everything. So no, there's nobody in my family who has ever had to go to a psychiatrist or be put in a hospital for their brain or anything like that. We're all just regular working people. We deal with physical stuff, like my dad's bad shoulder or my mom's back, or the pressure in the warehouse for me, but that's just life. There's no history of anything else.\n\nDoctor: Since this started, have you had any blood tests, brain scans, or other medical work-ups done, and if so, did any of them show anything abnormal?\n\nPatient: Medical work-ups? Brain scans? No, no, definitely nothing like that. Like I was telling you before, I had that one physical at the occupational clinic down on 4th Street before I got hired, where they made me pee in a cup for the drug screen and checked my blood pressure and everything, but that was months ago, way before any of this started. Since the air in the warehouse started getting so heavy and the pressure started pushing down on me in the aisles, I haven't been to any doctors or hospitals or clinics. \n\nI mean, why would I need a brain scan? My brain is completely fine. It's the environment that's the problem, the actual physical weight of the space I'm having to hold up. A blood test isn't going to show anything about that. \n\nBesides, I really don't have the time to go sit in some freezing cold waiting room reading five-year-old car magazines. Suddenly? No, no, it wasn't like I just woke up yesterday and everything was suddenly like this. It's been way longer than a few weeks, too. It’s been building up for a while... I mean, things have really been going downhill for about eleven months now.

It takes a lot of energy to hold up that kind of pressure. But it's not like my heart is just racing out of nowhere for no reason. It's just the exertion of dealing with the weight in the aisle. I actually had to do a full physical for this job—the company makes everyone go to this occupational clinic down on 4th Street before they even let you touch the forklift—and they checked all of that. I mean, I even started college, right? I was taking business administration classes before I took this break to work at the warehouse. It's like, recently, the air just gets really, really heavy, and my body just stops. My arms just go up on their own. I don't remember ever feeling that thickness in the air when I was little.
